scope.claims: 21 extracted records; colors describe this project's review coverage, not scientific truth.
scope.problems: Curated project questions drawn from existing reviews. These are not claims of newly discovered field-wide open problems.
scope.ranking: Curated starting order; no votes, funding or numerical value estimates have been fabricated.

claims.label: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)
claims.finding: Price and total-fitness variance are available. Additive genetic variance and the fixed-average-effect partial-change target are not established by our probe.
claims.next_action: Freeze genetic projection and partial-change semantics, then prove the missing correspondence.
claims.statement: The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.
claims.math: \Delta_{NS}\bar{w} = V_A(w)/\bar{w} (discrete generations); \left.\frac{d\bar{m}}{dt}\right|_{NS} = V_A(m) for Malthusian fitness m
claims.context: Assumptions: the 'partial change' holds average effects of alleles and the environment fixed (Price 1972, Ewens 1989); V_A is the additive genetic variance in fitness. Formal status: proved in this partial-change reading. Read as a claim about the total change in mean fitness it is false under dominance, epistasis, frequency dependence or a changing environment.
claims.source: Ronald A. Fisher (1930) The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection

claims.label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.
claims.math: Cov(z_i, z_j) = 2\Theta_{ij} V_A + \Delta_{ij} V_D; in the limit of M \to \infty loci the offspring trait given parents is Gaussian with mean (z_1+z_2)/2 and segregation variance V_0(1-\bar{F}), with error O(1/\sqrt{M}) (Barton, Etheridge and Veber 2017)
claims.context: Assumptions: many unlinked loci of small additive effect, random mating, environmental effects independent of genotype. Formal status: the covariance decomposition is proved; the infinitesimal limit, including under selection, is proved by Barton, Etheridge and Veber (2017). Large-effect loci and epistasis break the Gaussian limit.
claims.source: Ronald A. Fisher (1919) The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance

claims.label: Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene
claims.finding: The record already specifies logistic growth and warns that Allee effects change the speed.
claims.next_action: Specify kinetics and initial conditions before importing a front-speed formula.
claims.statement: An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.
claims.math: u_t = D u_{xx} + s u(1-u); travelling waves u(x-ct) exist iff c \ge c^* = 2\sqrt{sD}; compactly supported initial data spread at asymptotic speed c^*
claims.context: Assumptions: one spatial dimension (extended to R^n), constant diffusion D, logistic (genic) selection with coefficient s, deterministic large-population limit. Formal status: proved; Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov (1937) gave the proof independently, and Aronson and Weinberger (1978) proved the asymptotic spreading speed in several dimensions. Finite populations, Allee effects or long-tailed dispersal change the speed.
claims.source: Ronald A. Fisher (1937) The wave of advance of advantageous genes

claims.label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.
claims.math: ESS allocation: N_m c_m = N_f c_f; with c_m = c_f the unbeatable primary sex ratio is 1:1
claims.context: Assumptions: panmixia, autosomal control of the sex ratio, each offspring has one father and one mother, no local mate competition or sex-specific resource competition. Formal status: proved as an invasion (ESS) result (Shaw and Mohler 1953). Its own named exceptions (local mate competition, Hamilton 1967) are predicted deviations, not refutations.
claims.source: Ronald A. Fisher (1930) The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection

claims.label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
claims.math: with a singly mated queen, r_{sister,sister} = 3/4 > r_{mother,daughter} = 1/2, but r_{sister,brother} = 1/4
claims.context: Formal status: the relatedness coefficients are proved. The explanatory claim is largely abandoned: the low sister-brother relatedness offsets the gain unless the sex ratio is biased, diploid termites are eusocial, and comparative work points to ancestral monogamy instead (Hughes et al. 2008).
claims.source: W. D. Hamilton (1964) The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II

claims.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
claims.math: unbeatable proportion of males x^* = \frac{n-1}{2n} for n foundresses per patch (diploid case)
claims.context: Assumptions: n foundresses per patch, mating confined to the natal patch, only females disperse, mothers control the sex ratio. Formal status: proved as an ESS within the model. Haplodiploidy and inbreeding shift x* slightly.
claims.source: W. D. Hamilton (1967) Extraordinary Sex Ratios

claims.label: Hamilton's rule
claims.finding: The record explicitly uses regression coefficients. A witness with fixed causal payoff coefficients does not refute that identity.
claims.next_action: Review the genotype, transmission and regression mapping for the intended application.
claims.statement: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
claims.math: \Delta \bar{p} > 0 \iff r b - c > 0, with r, b, c defined as regression coefficients (Queller form via the Price equation)
claims.context: Assumptions: in Hamilton's original derivation, additive fitness effects and weak selection; in the general form, b and c are partial regressions of fitness on the actor's and the partner's genotype. Formal status: proved; exact in the regression form (Gardner, West and Wild 2011). Critics argue that the general form is close to an identity with little predictive content (Nowak, Tarnita and Wilson 2010).
claims.source: W. D. Hamilton (1964) The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I

claims.label: Declining force of selection with age
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
claims.math: s(a) = \frac{\partial r}{\partial \ln p_a} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{x=a+1}^{\infty} e^{-rx} l_x m_x, non-increasing in a
claims.context: Assumptions: an age-structured population with fixed age-specific fertility and no growth or repair after maturity. Formal status: the formula for s(a) is proved. The inevitability claim is refuted as stated: Jones et al. (2013) found species with flat or declining mortality with age, consistent with life histories where fertility rises with size.
claims.source: W. D. Hamilton (1966) The moulding of senescence by natural selection

claims.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
claims.finding: The record declares a diffusion approximation. The benchmark's finite haploid chain needs an explicit mapping to its diploid convention. Neutral fixation equals initial frequency exactly.
claims.next_action: Align ploidy and selection conventions, then compare the approximation with the specified finite chain.
claims.statement: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
claims.math: u(p) = \frac{1-e^{-4N_e s p}}{1-e^{-4N_e s}}; neutral limit u(p) = p, so a new mutant fixes with probability 1/(2N)
claims.context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, genic (additive) selection with coefficient s, constant effective size N_e, no linkage to other selected sites. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit.
claims.source: Motoo Kimura (1962) On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population

claims.label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
claims.math: \bar{t}_1(p) = -\frac{4N_e(1-p)\ln(1-p)}{p}; as p = 1/(2N) \to 0, \bar{t}_1 \to 4N_e generations
claims.context: Assumptions: diffusion approximation to the Wright-Fisher model, neutrality, constant N_e. Formal status: proved within the diffusion limit (Kimura and Ohta 1969).
claims.source: Motoo Kimura (1969) The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population

claims.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
claims.math: H = \frac{\theta}{1+\theta}, \theta = 4N_e\mu (infinite-alleles model)
claims.context: Assumptions: infinite-alleles mutation, neutrality, constant N_e, equilibrium. Formal status: proved within the model. Observed diversity varies far less across species than census sizes predict (Lewontin's paradox; Leffler et al. 2012), which points to linked selection and demography.
claims.source: Motoo Kimura (1964) The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population

claims.label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
claims.finding: The estimator is formalizable. A model proof alone cannot settle what fraction of substitutions in nature is neutral.
claims.next_action: Specify a population, data, estimator assumptions and a discriminating analysis.
claims.statement: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
claims.math: empirical claim: for most sites |N_e s| \lesssim 1, so the fraction of substitutions driven by positive selection \alpha is small; tested with d_N/d_S and McDonald-Kreitman \alpha = 1 - \frac{D_s P_n}{D_n P_s}
claims.context: Formal status: not a mathematical statement; an empirical claim about the distribution of fitness effects. King and Jukes (1969) proposed it independently. Genomic estimates of alpha and pervasive linked selection are cited against its strong form (Kern and Hahn 2018).
claims.source: Motoo Kimura (1968) Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level

claims.label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
claims.math: k = 2N\mu \cdot \frac{1}{2N} = \mu
claims.context: Assumptions: strictly neutral mutations, mutation rate constant per generation, steady state. Formal status: an exact consequence of the neutral fixation probability. Variation in generation time and weak selection on nearly neutral sites cause departures from strict clock-like rates.
claims.source: Motoo Kimura (1968) Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level

claims.label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
claims.math: I is an ESS iff for all J \ne I: E(I,I) > E(J,I), or E(I,I) = E(J,I) and E(I,J) > E(J,J); every ESS is an asymptotically stable rest point of the replicator dynamics (Taylor and Jonker 1978), not conversely
claims.context: Assumptions: an infinite, well-mixed population with pairwise interactions and asexual or clonal inheritance of strategies. Formal status: the definition is exact, and the link to replicator dynamics is proved. Finite populations, mutation and genetic constraints can stop an ESS from being reached.
claims.source: John Maynard Smith (1973) The Logic of Animal Conflict

claims.label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
claims.finding: The checked ESS calculation concerns the specified symmetric payoff matrix and 0 < V < C.
claims.next_action: Supply the payoff interpretation and test whether role asymmetries change the applicable game.
claims.statement: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
claims.math: payoffs E(H,H) = (V-C)/2, E(H,D) = V, E(D,H) = 0, E(D,D) = V/2; for C > V the unique ESS plays Hawk with probability p^* = V/C
claims.context: Assumptions: symmetric pairwise contests, fixed V and C, no role asymmetries (asymmetries such as ownership give the Bourgeois ESS instead). Formal status: proved within the game.
claims.source: John Maynard Smith (1982) Evolution and the Theory of Games

claims.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
claims.math: the relative heterozygosity H_{after}/H_{before} at a neutral site at recombination fraction c is an increasing function of c/s that tends to 0 as c/s \to 0; the affected region has a width of order s in recombination units, up to logarithmic factors in N
claims.context: Assumptions: a single sweep from a new mutation, deterministic allele-frequency trajectory, two loci. Formal status: proved under these approximations (later refined in coalescent treatments). Background selection produces a similar correlation between diversity and recombination.
claims.source: John Maynard Smith (1974) The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene

claims.label: Twofold cost of sex
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
claims.math: with equal fecundity and a 1:1 sex ratio, the odds of asexual to sexual females double each generation: \frac{q_{t+1}}{1-q_{t+1}} = 2\frac{q_t}{1-q_t}
claims.context: Assumptions: anisogamy with males contributing no resources, equal fecundity and viability of sexual and asexual females, a 1:1 sex ratio. Formal status: proved as a population-dynamic identity under these assumptions. Its biological force depends on how often those assumptions hold.
claims.source: John Maynard Smith (1978) The Evolution of Sex

claims.label: War of attrition ESS
claims.finding: This inventory contains no corresponding check. That does not mean the claim is unknown to science.
claims.next_action: Review the source-to-statement mapping, choose a precise target and record its acceptance conditions.
claims.statement: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
claims.math: with cost linear in time at unit rate and resource value V, the ESS persistence time has density p(x) = \frac{1}{V} e^{-x/V}
claims.context: Assumptions: symmetric contests, cost linear in display time, no information about the opponent's choice. Formal status: proved (Maynard Smith 1974); existence and uniqueness in the generalized game proved by Bishop and Cannings (1978).
claims.source: John Maynard Smith (1974) The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts

claims.label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
claims.finding: The continuum inequality does not ensure an unstable mode on a particular finite domain.
claims.next_action: Specify the domain and boundary conditions; check the determinant at admissible modes.
claims.statement: A homogeneous steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable to spatial perturbations when the chemicals diffuse at different rates, spontaneously producing a pattern.
claims.math:
u_t = f(u,v) + D_u 
abla^2 u, v_t = g(u,v) + D_v 
abla^2 v; with tr J < 0 and det J > 0, instability at some wavenumber k iff D_v f_u + D_u g_v > 2\sqrt{D_u D_v \det J}, which requires D_u 
e D_v
claims.context: Assumptions: two species, smooth kinetics, linearization about a homogeneous steady state, fixed domain without growth or mechanics. Formal status: the linear instability conditions are proved; existence and stability of nonlinear patterns are proved for many specific models but not in general.
claims.source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis

claims.label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
claims.finding: No single theorem target is specified here. A matching pattern alone does not identify its mechanism.
claims.next_action: Choose a biological system and measurements that distinguish reaction–diffusion from alternatives.
claims.statement: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
claims.math: no canonical formalization: the claim asserts that a biological pattern is generated by a system of the form u_t = F(u) + D\nabla^2 u with D not proportional to the identity
claims.context: Formal status: a framework rather than a mathematical proposition. Kondo and Asai (1995) confirmed the predicted stripe-branching dynamics in Pomacanthus and Castets et al. (1990) produced Turing patterns chemically. Mechanical buckling, prepatterns and cell-cell signalling can produce the same patterns, so a matching pattern alone does not identify the mechanism.
claims.source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis

claims.label: Turing wavelength selection
claims.finding: Near onset and large domain are already in the record. Our tolerance and finite-mode comparison are additional benchmark choices.
claims.next_action: Map the onset formula to a specified domain and distinguish a linear mode from the nonlinear selected pattern.
claims.statement: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
claims.math: at onset k_c^2 = \sqrt{\det J/(D_u D_v)}, \lambda_c = 2\pi/k_c; under uniform rescaling of D, \lambda \propto \sqrt{D}
claims.context: Assumptions: near onset of instability, two species, domain large compared with the wavelength. Formal status: proved by linear analysis. Away from onset, the selected wavelength depends on nonlinear terms and history.
claims.source: Alan Turing (1952) The chemical basis of morphogenesis

bridges.label: Shared Price route; Fisher genetic partition remains unestablished
Both require a specified admissible spectrum; not a proof edge
From mathematical mechanism to biological identification: measurements required
A checked special case does not establish the general target

problems.title: Connect the Price identity to Fisher's additive-genetic partial change
problems.known: The finite Price identity and a conditional Hamilton regression corollary have compiled. Total fitness variance is not generally additive genetic variance.
problems.question: Which explicit genetic projection and fixed-average-effect assumptions give a faithful Lean target for this extracted Fisher record?
problems.acceptance: Independent statement-fidelity review, exact target freeze, compiled projection/covariance correspondence, standard axiom audit and controls that distinguish total from additive variance.
problems.next_action: Specify the genetic projection and partial-change operation against primary sources before any prover run.
unlocks: Scoped reuse of the Price derivation
problems.cache: Reuse the existing Price proof and variance counterexample after checking exact types and assumptions.

problems.title: Determine what evidence could connect molecular predictions to tissue transport
problems.known: A protein structure prediction alone does not provide binding affinity, turnover or effective tissue diffusivity.
problems.question: For one specified biological system, what measured and modeled quantities are needed to evaluate a transport claim?
problems.acceptance: A source-linked dataset with matching biological context, explicit transport/kinetic model, held-out calibration and a stated remaining uncertainty or documented insufficiency of evidence.
problems.next_action: Choose a matched assay and audit the measured quantities before proposing a BioNeMo computation.
problems.cache: Reuse literature/data extraction and model outputs only when biological context and version match.

problems.title: Separate linear instability from the nonlinear pattern a simulation produces
problems.known: An admissible growing linear mode and a finite-time nonlinear pattern are different observables. Solver nonconvergence must remain visible.
problems.question: Within a frozen kinetics/domain/initial-condition ensemble, where do linear predictions and converged nonlinear outcomes differ?
problems.acceptance: Preregistered observables, amplitudes, horizons and tolerances; independent linear calculation; numerical convergence checks; unresolved cases reported; no universal biological threshold claim.
problems.next_action: Align the existing runner's observables and convergence categories before interpreting its movies or aggregates.
needs: bounded GPU resources only if useful
problems.cache: Reuse completed simulation arrays only with matching parameters, solver version and convergence receipt.

problems.title: Check that extracted claims preserve their source's actual meaning
problems.known: The 21-record audit checks hashes and copied fields. It does not establish faithfulness to original papers. Several records already state conditions that a short headline hides.
problems.question: Which source-to-record mappings preserve the mathematical object, quantifiers, units and scope?
problems.acceptance: Pinned source and passages, reviewed mapping of statement/math/context, explicit disagreements and versioned corrections. Citation presence alone is insufficient.
problems.next_action: Begin with Fisher and Hamilton, then release independent source-review shards for the remaining records.
problems.cache: Cache extraction and source passages with exact document/version references; retain correction history.

problems.title: Demonstrate one independent, useful reuse across participants
problems.known: Local self-tests and a coordination message do not demonstrate external reuse. Mycelium and other systems already provide close coordination precedents.
problems.question: Can a second participant inspect and reuse a scoped contribution to change a different research action?
problems.acceptance: Attributable second-participant run, exact consumed contribution version, applicability check, resulting artifact, independent review and measured overhead/cost.
problems.next_action: Agree the Delphi contribution format and offer one small replay or source-review task to an existing participant.
problems.cache: Reuse the reviewed contribution with its version, acceptance policy and scope; reject stale or incompatible reuse.

problems.title: Test whether attention and resource allocation improve useful progress
problems.known: Votes, agent count and post volume do not establish scientific progress. Agent-economy proposals already discuss resource and credit allocation.
problems.question: Which allocation rule improves accepted contributions or useful downstream decisions per constrained resource without starving exploration and replication?
problems.acceptance: Pinned task pool, separate interest/resource/blocking signals, preregistered utility and costs, expert-order and simple allocation baselines, coverage and failed/negative work included.
problems.next_action: Define the decision-maker's objective, acceptance predicates and resource constraints before choosing a voting or market mechanism.
problems.cache: Cache decisions, policy versions and outcomes; do not substitute reputational scores for evidence.

problems.title: Reject the volume-changing mode in the pinned liquid-bridge benchmark
problems.known: The n=1 sine displacement has nonzero integral and violates the stated fixed-volume constraint; independent review caught the benchmark interpretation before its agent evaluation.
problems.question: Which admissible perturbations preserve the declared bridge volume?
problems.acceptance: Exact integral witness and primary-source correspondence under the stated fixed-volume interpretation, recorded in the linked review.
problems.next_action: Reuse this review as a regression check when future benchmarks define admissible modes.
problems.cache: Retain the exact witness and source with the corrected boundary/volume assumptions.

mission.title: Engineer toward a flying fish
mission.scope: Authored from the flying-fish research report and checker handoff (see origin). Read levels are the report's own. Nothing here is an observation made by this site; derived numbers are labelled as arithmetic.

origin.note: Research report, 2026-10-31. Not tracked in this repository; the page restates its numbers and read-levels.
Checker handoff. The Python checker (71 tests) is not in this repository yet; this page reimplements its threshold table as browser arithmetic only.

scales.label: Molecular
scales.open: One molecule-to-fin source is indexed: Daane et al. 2021 shows a lat4a x kcnh2a interaction that phenocopies flying-fish fin proportion in zebrafish, with genome-wide association signatures across 35 species. The flying-fish side is association, not demonstration, and transfer to a halfbeak is an unestablished hypothesis. No parameter links it to wing area or loading.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling to macromolecular structure or to fin geometry.

scales.label: Macromolecular
scales.open: No structure or binding-affinity input for any fin-patterning protein. The stopped KCNE1 protocol shows what happens when a structure covers only 20.27% of an assay: the test is stopped, not run.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling to subcellular organisation.

scales.label: Subcellular
scales.open: Nothing indexed. Newer molecule-to-fin evidence (Daane 2021) is reported available but not yet in this snapshot.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling to cell behaviour.

scales.label: Cellular
scales.open: Daane et al. 2021 describes bioelectric and amino-acid-transport signalling that affects fin proportion in zebrafish; no exocoetid cell-level measurement is indexed. The bridge to exocoetid fins is unestablished.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling to tissue mechanics or patterning.

scales.label: Tissue
scales.open: Davenport (1992, abstract only) reports flying fish carry no more red axial muscle than a cruising mackerel, and that take-off acceleration probably needs anaerobic white muscle. No muscle power parameter enters any model here.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling from muscle tissue to launch speed.

scales.label: Organ
scales.open: Fin morphometrics are measured (pectoral fins supply 76-92% of wing area; hypocaudal lobe is 63.1 +/- 0.5% of caudal area). Only empirical allometry links fin size to mass; there is no model of how a fin forms or what loads it can bear.
scales.coupling_out: Empirical allometry only (Fish 1990 fits). Not a mechanistic coupling.

scales.label: Neural / control
scales.open: No source on taxiing, take-off or glide control is indexed. Whether a candidate can be stabilised by control rather than by geometry is an open question.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling to flight dynamics.

scales.label: Organism
scales.open: Wing loading, aspect ratio, glide distance and ground effect are measured or computed in the literature. Maximum L/D = 11.0 is a 1929 calculation relayed by Fish, not a measurement. Davenport 2003 (the maximum-size stability argument) has not been read.
scales.coupling_out: The browser calculation below is the only runnable organism-scale model; it is arithmetic on published fits, not a flight simulation.

scales.label: Developmental
scales.open: Juveniles under 0.05 m do not fly and their paired fins are hypothesised to be flotation organs (Hubbs 1933, relayed by Fish). How fin proportions emerge during growth is not modelled. The seeded Turing records are about pattern formation in general, not about fins.
scales.coupling_out: No executable coupling from developmental programme to adult morphometry.

scales.label: Collective
scales.open: Nothing indexed on schooling or group launch.

scales.label: Ecological / evolutionary
scales.open: The predator-escape hypothesis is Darwin's (1859) and, as far as the report's search reaches, has never been quantified, so it is not used as a constraint. Extant exocoetids stop at 50 cm total length (69 FishBase species with a parsed maximum), which is an observation about extant species and not a physical limit. The only exocoetid genome assembly is scaffold-level (GCA_018398805.1, Hirundichthys speculiger); no comparative exocoetid genomics is supportable.
scales.coupling_out: Reachability from a beloniform ancestor is NOT established by any check on this page. The developmental and evolutionary bridge to the organism scale is an open question.

couplings.text: Association only: lat4a x kcnh2a phenocopies fin proportion in zebrafish (Daane 2021); transfer to exocoetids is an unestablished hypothesis and no parameter maps it to wing area.
No executable model maps sequence change to structure or affinity for this mission.
No executable model from cell behaviour to fin or muscle tissue.
No executable model from tissue properties to fin geometry.
Fish (1990) allometric fits relate mass to wing loading per genus. Fitted coefficients, not mechanism; valid only inside the measured mass range.
No executable model from adult design back to a developmental programme.
Unestablished. A novel-appendage flag is metadata, not a reachability check; no model links developmental or evolutionary process to organism-scale design.

sources.cite: Fish, F. E. (1990). Wing design and scaling of flying fish with regard to flight performance. J. Zool. 221: 391-403.
sources.note: n = 199 preserved specimens, 33 species, 6 genera. The report read the extracted PDF text directly.
caveats: Text gives overall maximum pectoral aspect ratio 16.9; Table III gives Exocoetus 8.9-19.9. They disagree; both are shown.
Results text gives a 0.001 kg Hirundichthys as the lowest wing loading while the stated specimen range starts at 0.003 kg. Unresolved.
Re-read from the PDF (p.395) by the research lead: 3.0-16.9 is the INDIVIDUAL pectoral-fin aspect ratio; Table III reaches 19.9 for Exocoetus. Park & Choi measured 9.0-10.7 for the same quantity.

sources.cite: Park, H. & Choi, H. (2010). Aerodynamic characteristics of flying fish in gliding flight. J. Exp. Biol. 213(19): 3269-3279.
sources.read_level: full-text, as returned by a fetch tool
sources.note: Wind tunnel, Cypselurus hiraii models, Re = 1.9-2.2e4. Ground-effect drag reduction up to 14% over water. Maximum L/D numeric values appear only in figures and were not read.
caveats: Read through a fetch tool that summarises with a separate small model; not the same grade as text parsed directly.

sources.cite: Davenport, J. (1992). Wing-loading, stability and morphometric relationships in flying fish (Exocoetidae) from the North-eastern Atlantic. J. Mar. Biol. Assoc. UK 72(1): 25-39.
sources.read_level: abstract, as returned by a fetch tool
sources.note: Pectoral fin length cannot exceed 78-79% of standard length without impairing swimming. Pelvic fins of four-winged forms solve pitch stability. Oxyporhamphus micropterus has high wing loading but cannot take off because the centre of gravity lies behind the pectorals.
caveats: Full text paywalled; the DOI is as recorded by the report and was not opened for this page.
No URL is given: the DOI was not recorded in the report, and this page does not guess one.

sources.cite: Davenport, J. (2003). Allometric constraints on stability and maximum size in flying fishes: implications for their evolution. J. Fish Biol. 62(2): 455-463.
sources.note: NOT READ. The bibliographic record was confirmed; a third-party summary says larger fish place the centre of mass further behind the centre of wing pressure, capping two-winged size.
caveats: Wiley served a Cloudflare challenge. The size-limit argument is therefore not available as a constraint.

sources.cite: Lovejoy, N. R., Iranpour, M. & Collette, B. B. (2004). Phylogeny and jaw ontogeny of beloniform fishes. Integr. Comp. Biol. 44(5): 366-377. PMID 21676722.
sources.note: Supports monophyly of flyingfishes; flyingfishes are nested within a paraphyletic grade of halfbeaks.

sources.cite: Xu, G.-H., Zhao, L.-J., Gao, K.-Q. & Wu, F.-X. (2013). A new stem-neopterygian fish from the Middle Triassic of China shows the earliest over-water gliding strategy of the vertebrates. Proc. R. Soc. B 280(1750): 20122261.
sources.note: Bibliographic record verified against Crossref. Content (Potanichthys xingyiensis, a Triassic four-winged glider about 15 cm long) is from press and encyclopedia summaries, not the paper.
caveats: No URL is given: the DOI was not recorded in the report, and this page does not guess one.

sources.cite: Darwin, C. (1859). On the Origin of Species, Chapter VI. Project Gutenberg #1228 (also 22764, 2009).
sources.note: Darwin writes 'flying-fish' twice, as a conceivability argument ('our imaginary illustration'). He never writes 'Exocoetus' in the 1st, 2nd or 6th edition.
caveats: The printed page number of the first edition could not be obtained.
Editions 3-5 and other works (e.g. the Beagle journal) were not searched.

sources.cite: FishBase, Exocoetidae maximum lengths, scraped by the research report (2026-10-31).
sources.note: 116 Exocoetidae names; 69 returned a parsed maximum length, 10.3-50.0 cm (largest Cheilopogon japonicus, 50.0 cm TL). The halfbeak Hemiramphus brasiliensis reaches 55.0 cm TL.
caveats: Scraped values; not independently re-checked here.

sources.cite: Daane, J. M. et al. (2021). Curr. Biol. PMC9172250: lat4a x kcnh2a interaction phenocopying flying-fish fin proportion in zebrafish; genome-wide signatures across 35 species.
sources.note: A bioelectric and amino-acid-transport signalling interaction (lat4a, kcnh2a) that phenocopies flying-fish fin proportion in ZEBRAFISH, plus genome-wide signatures across 35 species. The functional demonstration is in zebrafish; the flying-fish side is association.
caveats: Cross-organism transfer: this does not establish that enlarging a halfbeak's fins is experimentally grounded. It is an unestablished transfer hypothesis.
A testable mechanism for a bigger paired fin; no flight is implied.
Title and author list are not restated here because the card did not carry them; only the journal, year and PMC id were given.

disagreements.title: Maximum pectoral aspect ratio: 16.9 or 19.9?

positions.says: Individual pectoral-fin AR 3.0 to 16.9, maximum in Exocoetus.

disagreements.handling: The AR check (C5) uses 16.9 and shows 19.9 as the alternative upper bound. A candidate between them is flagged, not passed or failed silently.

disagreements.title: Where does Oxyporhamphus belong?

positions.says: Sister to all other flyingfishes; subfamily Oxyporhamphinae resurrected.
Read as placing it with Hemiramphus and Euleptorhamphus, i.e. a halfbeak.

disagreements.handling: Unresolved and not read by the report. Whether the living functional intermediate is basal within gliders or a halfbeak changes what it is evidence for.

disagreements.title: Is there an upper size limit?

positions.says: Size is restricted by difficulty leaving the water, not by the wings.
That seems unlikely; larger fish can generate enough swimming power to leap.
Stability, not lift, bites: a fin-length ceiling and a centre of gravity moving aft of the centre of pressure.

disagreements.handling: No published number for a maximum body mass or length of a gliding fish could be verified. The page therefore reports a scaling argument and an observed extant-species envelope, not a limit.

mission.fit_note: WL = a M^b, WL in N/m^2, M in kg (Fish 1990 Table II, r.m.a. fits). The fits were measured on specimens up to 0.53 kg; anything above that is extrapolation and is flagged.

equations.name: Wing loading
equations.variables: M mass (kg), g = 9.81 m/s^2, S wing area (m^2: pectoral + pelvic fins + intervening body in Fish 1990).
equations.context: Definition. In this page's calculation S = b^2 / AR from the span and aspect ratio you enter, so S is a design input, not a measurement of a fish.

equations.name: Measured wing-loading allometry
equations.variables: Per-genus a, b from Fish 1990 Table II (see table). WL in N/m^2, M in kg.
equations.context: Empirical envelope for 0.003-0.53 kg specimens of six genera. It describes preserved specimens; it is not a mechanism and does not transfer outside that range.

equations.name: Level-flight speed scaling
equations.variables: rho air density, C_L lift coefficient. Fish 1990 cites Pennycuick (1972) that horizontal and vertical speeds go as the square root of wing loading.
equations.context: Steady, level, quasi-static lift balance L = W. Holds for fixed C_L. Taxi, launch and ground effect are outside this relation.

equations.name: Sink speed
equations.variables: V flight speed, L/D lift-to-drag ratio. The only L/D = 11.0 figure is Shoulejkin's (1929) calculation for Exocoetus volitans, relayed by Fish; Fish gives 1.4 m/s at 15 m/s.
equations.context: Relation between glide ratio and sink speed. The L/D value is a relayed calculation, not a measurement.

equations.name: Aspect ratio
equations.context: Definition. Fish 1990: individual pectoral-fin AR 3.0-16.9; birds, bats and insects average about 7; albatrosses about 15.

equations.name: Launch-speed anchor used by the check
equations.variables: Anchored at 16 m/s for WL = 205.5 N/m^2 (the largest Cypselurus loading Fish measured; observed Cypselurus take-off speeds are 16-20 m/s).
equations.context: A scaling rule with a single anchor point, not a fit. Moderate confidence per the checker handoff.

constraints.name: Wing-loading envelope
constraints.confidence: High empirically; moderate as a limit
constraints.note: The largest wing loading measured on any specimen across six genera (Danichthys; the Cypselurus maximum is 205.5). Genus context matters: a candidate is not a Danichthys unless stated. Exceeding it is outside what has been observed, not proof of impossibility.

constraints.name: Launch speed implied by loading (Cypselurus taxi anchor)
constraints.rule: IF the taxi-speed assumption is opted in: declared speed >= 16 sqrt(WL/205.5) m/s
constraints.confidence: Moderate at best; a Cypselurus taxiing launch speed, not a universal flight bound
constraints.note: The 16-20 m/s figures are observed Cypselurus taxi/launch speeds. Applying them as a flight-speed requirement for any design is an opt-in assumption, off by default.

constraints.name: Pectoral fin length
constraints.note: Davenport (1992, abstract) reports swimming is impaired beyond about 78-79% of standard length. Treat it as a reported envelope, not a demonstrated ceiling.

constraints.name: Longitudinal stability (qualitative flag only)
constraints.rule: source-assigned qualitative CG statement; never a green pass
constraints.confidence: Qualitative; no numeric centre-of-gravity data exist
constraints.note: Davenport reports CG-behind-pectorals as why Oxyporhamphus cannot take off. Without a numeric CG offset and a threshold the page cannot return a pass; it can only show the flag. Davenport 2003 is unread. No measured centre-of-gravity number exists for any exocoetid; Oxyporhamphus is the one living illustration.

constraints.name: Aspect-ratio envelope (opt-in assumption)
constraints.rule: IF the fin-level AR assumption is opted in: 3.0 <= AR <= 16.9 (19.9 in Fish Table III)
constraints.confidence: Moderate for individual pectoral fins; unestablished for a whole wing
constraints.note: Fish's 3.0-16.9 is the aspect ratio of individual pectoral fins. This page's AR is span squared over whole-wing area. Treating them as the same is an assumption, off by default.

constraints.name: Novel-appendage flag (metadata only)
constraints.rule: a declared novel appendage or powered flapping is flagged; absence of a flag establishes nothing
constraints.confidence: Metadata only. NOT a reachability check
constraints.note: A dorsal wing, jointed or flapping wing, novel skeletal element or sustained powered flapping falls outside the route sourced from the exocoetid literature (enlarged fin rays plus an axial/tail launch motor; flyingfishes nested in halfbeaks). That means unsupported by the sourced envelope: state your mechanism. It does not mean impossible. No check on this page establishes reachability; the developmental and evolutionary bridge is unestablished.

constraints.name: Extant-species size envelope
constraints.confidence: High for extant species; low as a physical limit
constraints.note: Observed over 69 extant Exocoetidae with a parsed maximum (10.3-50.0 cm TL). Not a physical bound.

constraints.name: Ontogenetic gliding threshold
constraints.note: Juveniles under 0.05 m do not fly (Hubbs 1933, relayed by Fish).

presets.name: Nothing declared
presets.note: Every check returns cannot-evaluate. This is the correct answer when nothing is known.

presets.name: Cypselurus-type, 0.1 kg
presets.note: Wing loading and area are arithmetic from Fish 1990 Table II (a = 285.015, b = 0.400) at 0.1 kg. Standard length is isometric scaling of the report's 0.37 m at 0.53 kg. Aspect ratio 10 is illustrative, inside the measured 3.0-16.9. Not a measured fish.

presets.name: Scaled-up Cypselurus, 5 kg
presets.note: Same arithmetic extrapolated to 5 kg; the report puts implied standard length at 0.82 m. Everything here lies beyond the measured mass range.

presets.name: Oxyporhamphus-like (CG aft)
presets.note: Davenport describes Oxyporhamphus micropterus as high wing loading with the centre of gravity too far aft to take off. Mass and wing area are withheld because no source read gives them as numbers.

mission.extrapolation_table_note: Browser arithmetic on the Cypselurus fit; extrapolates beyond the 0.53 kg maximum measured. The fit crosses 500 N/m^2, about 2.4x anything measured, near 4 kg.

engineering_questions.title: Turn Davenport (2003) into a real size bound
engineering_questions.known: There is a documented scaling argument (wing loading rises as M^0.36-0.53) and a documented stability argument, but no verified numeric maximum body mass or length for a gliding fish. Davenport 2003 is the paper that argues a maximum size and it has not been read.
engineering_questions.question: What maximum size, if any, does the stability argument give, and for which design (two- or four-winged)?
engineering_questions.settles_by: Read the paper at full-text grade; encode its relation as a named constraint with its derivation population; show a candidate on each side of it.
engineering_questions.next_action: Obtain Davenport (2003) past the publisher's bot challenge by a legitimate route and read it.
needs: full-text access to J. Fish Biol. 62(2):455-463

engineering_questions.title: Find raw exocoetid fin-area and mass data
engineering_questions.known: Fish (1990) publishes fitted coefficients, not specimen data, so uncertainty on the wing-loading envelope cannot be recomputed. Dryad, Figshare, Zenodo and MorphoBank were not searched by name.
engineering_questions.question: Does a raw morphometric dataset pairing pectoral fin area with body mass exist for Exocoetidae?
engineering_questions.settles_by: A dataset with accession, licence and checksum, retrieved and replayed against the published fits; or a documented negative search.
engineering_questions.next_action: Search the four named repositories and record the queries and results either way.

engineering_questions.title: Resolve the aspect-ratio upper bound
engineering_questions.known: Fish (1990) text says the maximum individual pectoral-fin aspect ratio is 16.9; Table III gives 19.9 for Exocoetus. Both are in the same paper.
engineering_questions.question: Which is correct, and which does the AR constraint (C5) rest on?
engineering_questions.settles_by: Read Table III and the text against each other, or the original specimen data (see EQ2).
engineering_questions.next_action: Re-read the table in the PDF by eye and record which figure a specimen supports.

engineering_questions.title: Couple fin morphometry to a mechanism, not only a fit
engineering_questions.known: The organ-to-organism link is Fish's allometric fits. They are valid inside 0.003-0.53 kg and carry no mechanism.
engineering_questions.question: What model would relate fin tissue and development to fin area and loading so a candidate outside the measured range can be assessed?
engineering_questions.settles_by: A coupling record with units, parameter transfer assumptions and an independent check, per SPEC-005.
engineering_questions.next_action: Specify the variables and ports on both sides before any model run.

engineering_questions.title: Is a numeric L/D measurable from the existing wind-tunnel work?
engineering_questions.known: The only maximum L/D = 11.0 is Shoulejkin's 1929 calculation for Exocoetus volitans. Park & Choi report maximum L/D near level flight, with values only in figures.
engineering_questions.question: What L/D does a four-winged Cypselurus model reach, with what Re and uncertainty?
engineering_questions.settles_by: Numeric L/D read from the paper's figures or data, or a recorded simulation with a convergence check; the sink-speed relation then uses a sourced value.
engineering_questions.next_action: Obtain the figure data from the paper and record the read-level.

engineering_questions.title: Does the lat4a x kcnh2a fin mechanism transfer from zebrafish to a halfbeak or flying fish?
engineering_questions.known: Daane et al. 2021 phenocopy flying-fish fin proportion with a lat4a x kcnh2a interaction in zebrafish and report genome-wide signatures across 35 species. The flying-fish side is association.
engineering_questions.question: What measurement in a beloniform would show the same mechanism sets paired-fin size, and how much fin enlargement would it explain?
engineering_questions.settles_by: A pre-specified measurement in a beloniform (or a documented negative), with organism context stated, linked to a fin-area parameter with units.
engineering_questions.next_action: Specify the beloniform measurement and what a null result would mean before any experiment or data pull.
needs: comparative genomics access (only one scaffold-level exocoetid assembly exists)
engineering_questions.origin: Daane 2021 card from the research lead; cross-organism transfer flagged as unestablished

goal.title: Engineer toward a flying fish
goal.text: Design requirement: a vertebrate glider reachable from a beloniform ancestor that satisfies the constraints below at a stated mass. The goal does not assert that such a design is feasible.
